title: Burnside Counting Lemma from Orbit-Stabilizer
description: The Burnside counting lemma (Cauchy-Frobenius) follows from the orbit-stabilizer theorem, which generalizes Lagrange's theorem. The chain: Lagrange -> Orbit-Stabilizer -> Burnside.

overview.historicalContext: Lagrange's theorem — that the order of any subgroup divides the order of a finite group — appeared in Lagrange's 1771 study of permutation groups and algebraic equations, a precursor to group theory itself. The orbit-stabilizer theorem emerged from 19th-century developments by Galois, Cauchy, and others. 'Burnside's lemma' is a mathematical misnomer: the counting formula $|X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}|\operatorname{Fix}(g)|$ was proved by Cauchy (1845) and independently rediscovered by Frobenius (1887). Burnside only popularized it in his 1897 textbook 'Theory of Groups of Finite Order' — and even there attributed it to Frobenius. The misattribution became standard usage despite Burnside's own acknowledgment. The lemma became a fundamental tool in combinatorial enumeration — counting equivalence classes of objects under symmetry — and was extended by Polya in 1937 to the full enumeration theorem using cycle index polynomials.
overview.problemStatement:
Can the Burnside counting lemma be formalized as a consequence of the orbit-stabilizer theorem, which itself generalizes Lagrange?

**Answer: Yes.** All three results are in Mathlib and the chain is formalized explicitly.
overview.text: Burnside's counting lemma follows from orbit-stabilizer, which generalizes Lagrange's theorem.
overview.proofStrategy: Wrap Mathlib's group action machinery to show the explicit chain: Lagrange -> Orbit-Stabilizer -> Burnside Counting Lemma.
keyInsights: The chain Lagrange → Orbit-Stabilizer → Burnside is a prototypical example of how a basic divisibility result (subgroup orders divide group order) underpins powerful combinatorial counting via a two-step generalization
Orbit-stabilizer IS Lagrange: since Stab(x) ≤ G is a subgroup and Orb(x) ≃ G/Stab(x), Lagrange's index form |G| = [G:Stab(x)] · |Stab(x)| gives |Orb(x)| · |Stab(x)| = |G| directly
Burnside's lemma follows from a double-counting argument: counting {(g,x) : g·x = x} two ways gives Σ|Fix(g)| = Σ|Stab(x)| = (orbit-stabilizer) |G| · |X/G|
The integer form Σ|Fix(g)| = |X/G|·|G| avoids division by |G|, making the statement cleaner to formalize in ℕ and verify in Lean without requiring |G| ≠ 0

Despite being called 'Burnside's lemma,' the result was proved by Cauchy (1845) and Frobenius (1887); Burnside himself attributed it to Frobenius in his 1897 textbook — a recurring pattern of mathematical misattribution

conclusion.summary: The Burnside counting lemma is formalized as a direct consequence of the orbit-stabilizer theorem, which itself generalizes Lagrange's theorem. The chain Lagrange -> Orbit-Stabilizer -> Burnside is made explicit.
conclusion.implications: Shows how a basic divisibility result (Lagrange) underpins powerful combinatorial counting tools (Burnside) through the intermediate structural result (orbit-stabilizer).
openQuestions: Can Polya's enumeration theorem (1937) be formalized as a generalization of Burnside's lemma, incorporating weights via cycle index polynomials? This would require formalizing the cycle structure of permutations acting on colorings.

How does the weighted Burnside's lemma connect to representation theory? The formula |X/G| = (1/|G|) Σ_g |Fix(g)| is the inner product of the trivial character with the permutation character, suggesting a character-theoretic proof and generalization.

Can Burnside's lemma be applied directly in Lean to enumerate concrete combinatorial objects — e.g., counting distinct binary necklaces of length n or colorings of a regular polygon under rotation and reflection?
